title: An Introduction to Restricted Mean Survival Time (RMST)
text:
An Introduction to Restricted Mean Survival Time (RMST) Author Akif Mustafa ✉ Published June 1, 2026 1 Introduction The Cox proportional hazards (CPH) model is the go-to model for survival analysis. It is popular for good reasons: It is semi-parametric — no distributional assumption needed. It handles multiple predictor variables. It gives an easy-to-interpret summary: the hazard ratio (HR) . It handles censoring naturally. But it makes one strong assumption: proportional hazards (PH) . This means the hazard of the event in two groups must always remain proportional throughout the study period. Everything works well when this holds. What if it does not hold? When hazards are not proportional — for example, when survival curves cross, when there is a delayed treatment effect, or when the benefit diminishes over time — a single HR becomes misleading. It no longer summarizes the treatment effect well. Potential hazard scenarious In these situations, there are several analytical alternatives to the standard Cox model: Piecewise Cox model Cox model with time-varying coefficients Royston-Parmar parametric model Accelerated failure time (AFT) model Cure models Restricted Mean Survival Time (RMST) is one such alternative. It is practical, interpretable, and widely used when the proportional hazards assumption is violated. 2 What is RMST? The Restricted Mean Survival Time (RMST) up to a time point \(	au\) is: The average time a person survives from time 0 to time \(	au\) . Equivalently, the area under the survival curve \(S(t)\) from 0 to \(	au\) . Mathematically: \[ 	ext{RMST}(	au) = E[\min(T, 	au)] = \int_0^{	au} S(t)\, dt \] Two key points: “Restricted” means we only look up to a pre-specified horizon \(	au\) (e.g., 5 years), not to infinity. It is a non-parametric summary of the whole survival curve up to \(	au\) . No proportional hazards assumption. No specific model required. 2.1 Visualizing RMST: Area Under the Curve Code set.seed ( 1 ) tau <- 48 t_seq <- seq ( 0 , 60 , by = 0.1 ) s_t <- exp ( - 0.03 * t_seq) df_line <- data.frame ( time = t_seq, surv = s_t) df_shade <- data.frame ( time = c ( 0 , t_seq[t_seq <= tau], tau), surv = c ( 0 , s_t[t_seq <= tau], 0 ) ) ggplot () + geom_polygon ( data = df_shade, aes (time, surv), fill = "steelblue" , alpha = 0.35 ) + geom_line ( data = df_line, aes (time, surv), color = "steelblue" , linewidth = 1.2 ) + geom_vline ( xintercept = tau, linetype = "dashed" , color = "black" ) + annotate ( "text" , x = tau + 1.5 , y = 0.85 , label = expression (tau), size = 5 , hjust = 0 ) + annotate ( "text" , x = tau / 2.5 , y = 0.22 , label = "RMST = Area 
 under S(t) 
 up to τ" , size = 3.8 , color = "steelblue4" , fontface = "bold" ) + labs ( title = "Restricted Mean Survival Time (RMST)" , subtitle = paste0 ( "Shaded area = RMST up to τ = " , tau, " months" ), x = "Time (months)" , y = "Survival probability S(t)" ) + scale_x_continuous ( breaks = seq ( 0 , 60 , 12 )) + scale_y_continuous ( limits = c ( 0 , 1 ), breaks = seq ( 0 , 1 , 0.2 )) + theme_classic ( base_size = 12 ) RMST is the area under the survival curve S(t) from time 0 to τ 2.2 RMST for Two Groups For two groups (e.g., treatment vs. control), the difference in RMST is the area between the two survival curves from 0 to \(	au\) . It tells you: on average, how much extra survival time does the treatment provide up to time \(	au\) ? Code set.seed ( 2 ) tau <- 48 t_seq <- seq ( 0 , 60 , by = 0.1 ) s_trt <- exp ( - 0.020 * t_seq) s_ctrl <- exp ( - 0.035 * t_seq) df_two <- data.frame ( time = t_seq, Treated = s_trt, Control = s_ctrl ) |> tidyr :: pivot_longer ( - time, names_to = "Group" , values_to = "Survival" ) df_between <- data.frame ( time = c (t_seq[t_seq <= tau], rev (t_seq[t_seq <= tau])), surv = c (s_trt[t_seq <= tau], rev (s_ctrl[t_seq <= tau])) ) ggplot () + geom_polygon ( data = df_between, aes (time, surv), fill = "gold" , alpha = 0.5 ) + geom_line ( data = df_two, aes (time, Survival, color = Group), linewidth = 1.2 ) + geom_vline ( xintercept = tau, linetype = "dashed" , color = "black" ) + annotate ( "text" , x = tau + 1.5 , y = 0.9 , label = expression (tau), size = 5 , hjust = 0 ) + annotate ( "text" , x = 15 , y = 0.55 , label = "RMST 
 Difference" , size = 3.8 , color = "darkgoldenrod" , fontface = "bold" ) + scale_color_manual ( values = c ( "Control" = "tomato" , "Treated" = "steelblue" )) + labs ( title = "RMST Difference Between Two Groups" , subtitle = "Shaded area = difference in RMST up to τ" , x = "Time (months)" , y = "Survival probability S(t)" ) + scale_x_continuous ( breaks = seq ( 0 , 60 , 12 )) + scale_y_continuous ( limits = c ( 0 , 1 ), breaks = seq ( 0 , 1 , 0.2 )) + theme_classic ( base_size = 12 ) + theme ( legend.position = "bottom" ) RMST difference = shaded area between the two survival curves up to τ 3 Why RMST? Limitations of the Cox Model The Cox model gives hazard ratios. HRs are useful, but they have real limitations. 3.1 PH Assumption The Cox model requires proportional hazards . If hazards are not proportional (crossing curves, delayed effects, diminishing benefits), a single HR is misleading. In immuno-oncology, for example, survival curves often separate late or cross altogether. The PH assumption frequently fails here. 3.2 HR is Relative, Not Absolute HR = 0.6 means a 40% lower hazard. But what does that mean in months of life gained ? That depends on the baseline hazard — a detail HR does not convey. Clinicians and patients often more interested in: “How much extra time do I get, on average?” than about a hazard ratio. 3.3 HR is Model-Based The Cox HR is a model-based summary. If the model is wrong — due to non-proportional hazards or misspecification — the HR can be biased and difficult to interpret. 3.4 How RMST Addresses These Limitations Issue Cox HR RMST Requires PH assumption ✅ Yes ❌ No Absolute effect size ❌ No ✅ Yes (time gained) Model-free ❌ No ✅ Yes (from KM curve) Easy clinical communication ⚠️ Moderate ✅ High RMST is not a replacement for the Cox model in all settings. It is a complement and an alternative — especially when PH fails or an absolute effect size matters more. 4 When to Use RMST? 4.1 Use RMST When: 1. Non-proportional hazards (NPH) are present Crossing survival curves Delayed treatment effect (early overlap, later separation) Diminishing benefit (early benefit that later fades) 2. An absolute effect is more meaningful than a relative one “Patients in the active arm survive on average 3 months longer over 5 years.” Health economics: quantifying life-years gained within a fixed horizon. 3. You want a model-free summary No reliance on a correctly specified Cox model. Simple, robust comparison of two survival curves up to \(	au\) . 4. As a supplement to HRs and log-rank tests Even when PH holds, RMST can be reported alongside the HR to provide an absolute effect estimate. Many recent clinical trials in oncology report both HR and RMST difference. 4.2 You Probably Do Not Need RMST When: PH holds well, and HR is sufficient for your scientific or clinical question, and There is no strong demand for an absolute “time gained” interpretation. 5 Estimation 5.1 Single Group The steps are straightforward: Estimate the survival curve \(S(t)\) using the Kaplan–Meier estimator. Choose a clinically relevant truncation time \(	au\) (e.g., 5 years). Pre-specify this before the analysis. Compute the area under the KM curve from 0 to \(	au\) using the trapezoidal rule (sum of rectangles under the step function). Estimate the standard error using a Greenwood-type formula. Construct confidence intervals using asymptotic normality (for large samples). 5.2 Two-Group Comparison Let \(S_1(t)\) and \(S_0(t)\) be the KM curves in the treatment and control groups. \[ 	ext{RMST}_1(	au) = \int_0^{	au} S_1(t)\, dt \qquad 	ext{RMST}_0(	au) = \int_0^{	au} S_0(t)\, dt \] Three key summary measures: 1. Difference in RMST (most common) \[ \Delta(	au) = 	ext{RMST}_1(	au) - 	ext{RMST}_0(	au) = \int_0^{	au} [S_1(t) - S_0(t)]\, dt \] Interpretation : On average, how many extra months does treatment provide by time \(	au\) ? 2. Ratio of RMST \[  rac{	ext{RMST}_1(	au)}{	ext{RMST}_0(	au)} \] Interpretation : Relative increase in average survival time up to \(	au\) . 3. Ratio of Restricted Mean Time Lost (RMTL) \[ 	ext{RMTL}(	au) = 	au - 	ext{RMST}(	au) \] This is the average time lost due to the event before \(	au\) . \[ 	ext{RMTL ratio} =  rac{	ext{RMTL}_1(	au)}{	ext{RMTL}_0(	au)} \] Interpretation : Useful when the focus is on time lost rather than time lived. Inference (difference and ratio): Based on asymptotic normality with Greenwood-based variance estimates. Provides standard errors, confidence intervals, and p-values. 6 Choosing \(	au\) The choice of \(	au\) matters. Some guidance: \(	au\) should be clinically chosen and pre-specified before the analysis (e.g., 5-year RMST in a cancer trial). It must fall within the observed follow-up where enough events have occurred and the KM estimate is reliable (i.e., do not extrapolate beyond the last event time). A common practical rule: set \(	au\) at or before the minimum of the two groups’ last event times , or at a clinically meaningful landmark such as 1, 2, or 5 years. Some methods choose \(	au\) adaptively, but a fixed, pre-specified \(	au\) is preferred for transparency and interpretability. Effect of τ choice on RMST estimation. The shaded areas show RMST for three different values of τ. 7 Example in R Here we simulate a delayed treatment effect: Before 12 months: treatment and control have similar hazard. After 12 months: treatment hazard becomes lower. This violates proportional hazards. 7.1 Simulate Data Code library (survival) library (survRM2) library (ggplot2) library (dplyr) library (tibble) library (knitr) library (kableExtra) set.seed ( 999 ) n <- 600 arm <- rbinom (n, 1 , 0.5 ) # 0 = control, 1 = treatment # Control: constant hazard throughout t_control <- rexp (n, rate = 0.05 ) # Treatment: same hazard before 12 months, lower hazard after 12 months t1 <- rexp (n, rate = 0.05 ) t_treat <- ifelse (t1 < 12 , t1, 12 + rexp (n, rate = 0.02 )) time_event <- ifelse (arm == 0 , t_control, t_treat) # Administrative censoring at 36 months time <- pmin (time_event, 36 ) status <- as.integer (time_event <= 36 ) dat <- tibble ( time = time, status = status, arm = factor (arm, levels = c ( 0 , 1 ), labels = c ( "Control" , "Treatment" )) ) # Summary table dat |> group_by (arm) |> summarise ( N = n (), Events = sum (status), Censored = N - Events, Max_followup = round ( max (time), 1 ), .groups = "drop" ) |> kable ( caption = "Summary of simulated dataset" , col.names = c ( "Group" , "N" , "Events" , "Censored" , "Max Follow-up (months)" ) ) |> kable_styling ( bootstrap_options = c ( "striped" , "hover" , "condensed" ), full_width = FALSE ) Summary of simulated dataset Group N Events Censored Max Follow-up (months) Control 302 248 54 36 Treatment 298 208 90 36 7.2 Kaplan–Meier Curves Code fit_km <- survfit ( Surv (time, status) ~ arm, data = dat) # Extract KM step data for ggplot km_df <- data.frame ( time = fit_km $ time, surv = fit_km $ surv, strata = rep ( names (fit_km $ strata), fit_km $ strata) ) |> mutate ( arm = sub ( "arm=" , "" , strata)) # Add time = 0 rows for each group time0 <- data.frame ( time = 0 , surv = 1 , strata = NA , arm = c ( "Control" , "Treatment" ) ) km_plot_df <- bind_rows (time0, km_df) |> arrange (arm, time) ggplot (km_plot_df, aes ( x = time, y = surv, color = arm)) + geom_step ( linewidth = 1 ) + scale_color_manual ( name = "Group" , values = c ( "Control" = "tomato" , "Treatment" = "steelblue" ) ) + scale_x_continuous ( limits = c ( 0 , 36 ), breaks = seq ( 0 , 36 , 6 )) + scale_y_continuous ( limits = c ( 0 , 1 ), breaks = seq ( 0 , 1 , 0.2 )) + labs ( title = "Kaplan–Meier Curves: Delayed Treatment Effect" , subtitle = "Curves overlap early and diverge after ~12 months" , x = "Time (months)" , y = "Survival probability" ) + theme_classic ( base_size = 12 ) + theme ( legend.position = "bottom" ) Kaplan–Meier curves for simulated delayed treatment effect data The curves initially overlap, reflecting similar early hazards. After 12 months they diverge as the treatment arm benefits from a lower hazard. This pattern suggests a violation of the proportional hazards assumption. 7.3 Check the Proportional Hazards Assumption 7.3.1 First, lets fit the cox PH model Code cox_fit <- coxph ( Surv (time, status) ~ arm, data = dat) summary (cox_fit) Call: coxph(formula = Surv(time, status) ~ arm, data = dat) n= 600, number of events= 456 coef exp(coef) se(coef) z Pr(>|z|) armTreatment -0.23982 0.78677 0.09429 -2.543 0.011 * --- Signif. codes: 0 '***' 0.001 '**' 0.01 '*' 0.05 '.' 0.1 ' ' 1 exp(coef) exp(-coef) lower .95 upper .95 armTreatment 0.7868 1.271 0.654 0.9465 Concordance= 0.518 (se = 0.013 ) Likelihood ratio test= 6.5 on 1 df, p=0.01 Wald test = 6.47 on 1 df, p=0.01 Score (logrank) test = 6.5 on 1 df, p=0.01 7.3.2 Now, check the PH assumption using schoenfeld test Code zph <- cox.zph (cox_fit) # Print test result as a neat table as.data.frame (zph $ table) |> kable ( caption = "Schoenfeld residuals test for proportional hazards" , digits = 4 ) |> kable_styling ( bootstrap_options = c ( "striped" , "hover" , "condensed" ), full_width = FALSE ) Schoenfeld residuals test for proportional hazards chisq df p arm 8.4937 1 0.0036 GLOBAL 8.4937 1 0.0036 A p-value below 0.05 on the Schoenfeld test indicates a violation of the PH assumption. 7.3.3 Plot the Schoenfeld residuals for visual inspection Code plot (zph, main = "Schoenfeld Residuals Over Time" ) abline ( h = 0 , lty = 2 , col = "grey50" ) Scaled Schoenfeld residuals. A flat line suggests PH holds; a trend suggests violation. A non-linear trend in the residuals plot confirms this. PH is violated here — making RMST a better choice. 7.4 Compute RMST We use the survRM2 package and set \(	au = 36\) months. Code tau_val <- 36 rm <- rmst2 ( time = dat $ time, status = dat $ status, arm = as.integer (dat $ arm == "Treatment" ), # 1 = treatment, 0 = control tau = tau_val ) rm The truncation time: tau = 36 was specified. Restricted Mean Survival Time (RMST) by arm Est. se lower .95 upper .95 RMST (arm=1) 18.613 0.804 17.038 20.189 RMST (arm=0) 16.722 0.716 15.319 18.125 Restricted Mean Time Lost (RMTL) by arm Est. se lower .95 upper .95 RMTL (arm=1) 17.387 0.804 15.811 18.962 RMTL (arm=0) 19.278 0.716 17.875 20.681 Between-group contrast Est. lower .95 upper .95 p RMST (arm=1)-(arm=0) 1.891 -0.218 4.001 0.079 RMST (arm=1)/(arm=0) 1.113 0.988 1.254 0.078 RMTL (arm=1)/(arm=0) 0.902 0.803 1.013 0.082 7.4.1 Results Tables Code arm1_vec <- unlist (rm $ RMST.arm1) arm0_vec <- unlist (rm $ RMST.arm0) rmst_trt_est <- as.numeric (arm1_vec[ 1 ]) rmst_trt_lo <- as.numeric (arm1_vec[ 2 ]) rmst_trt_hi <- as.numeric (arm1_vec[ 3 ]) rmst_ctrl_est <- as.numeric (arm0_vec[ 1 ]) rmst_ctrl_lo <- as.numeric (arm0_vec[ 2 ]) rmst_ctrl_hi <- as.numeric (arm0_vec[ 3 ]) rmst_summary <- data.frame ( Group = c ( "Treatment" , "Control" ), RMST = c (rmst_trt_est, rmst_ctrl_est), Lower = c (rmst_trt_lo, rmst_ctrl_lo), Upper = c (rmst_trt_hi, rmst_ctrl_hi) ) rmst_summary |> kable ( caption = paste0 ( "RMST estimates up to τ = " , tau_val, " months" ), col.names = c ( "Group" , "RMST (months)" , "95% CI Lower" , "95% CI Upper" ), digits = 2 ) |> kable_styling ( bootstrap_options = c ( "striped" , "hover" , "condensed" ), full_width = FALSE ) RMST estimates up to τ = 36 months Group RMST (months) 95% CI Lower 95% CI Upper Treatment 18.61 17.39 0.80 Control 16.72 19.28 0.72 7.4.2 Contrast Table Code contrast_df <- as.data.frame (rm $ unadjusted.result) contrast_df $ Measure <- c ( "RMST Difference (Treatment - Control)" , "RMST Ratio (Treatment / Control)" , "RMTL Ratio (Treatment / Control)" ) contrast_df <- contrast_df[, c ( "Measure" , "Est." , "lower .95" , "upper .95" , "p" )] contrast_df |> kable ( caption = "RMST contrast measures" , col.names = c ( "Measure" , "Estimate" , "95% CI Lower" , "95% CI Upper" , "P-value" ), digits = c ( 0 , 2 , 2 , 2 , 4 ) ) |> kable_styling ( bootstrap_options = c ( "striped" , "hover" , "condensed" ), full_width = FALSE ) RMST contrast measures Measure Estimate 95% CI Lower 95% CI Upper P-value RMST (arm=1)-(arm=0) RMST Difference (Treatment - Control) 1.89 -0.22 4.00 0.0789 RMST (arm=1)/(arm=0) RMST Ratio (Treatment / Control) 1.11 0.99 1.25 0.0780 RMTL (arm=1)/(arm=0) RMTL Ratio (Treatment / Control) 0.90 0.80 1.01 0.0816 7.5 Visualize RMST Code # Fit separate KM curves for each arm km_trt <- survfit ( Surv (time, status) ~ 1 , data = filter (dat, arm == "Treatment" )) km_ctrl <- survfit ( Surv (time, status) ~ 1 , data = filter (dat, arm == "Control" )) # Helper: convert survfit object to a step-function data frame km_to_df <- function (km_obj, group_label) { data.frame ( time = c ( 0 , km_obj $ time), surv = c ( 1 , km_obj $ surv), group = group_label ) } df_trt <- km_to_df (km_trt, "Treatment" ) df_ctrl <- km_to_df (km_ctrl, "Control" ) # Helper: build a closed polygon for shading up to tau make_shade <- function (df, tau_limit) { # Keep only time points up to tau df_trunc <- df[df $ time <= tau_limit, ] # Add a closing point at tau with the last survival value df_trunc <- rbind (df_trunc, data.frame ( time = tau_limit, surv = tail (df_trunc $ surv, 1 ), group = df_trunc $ group[ 1 ])) # Close the polygon back to zero data.frame ( time = c ( 0 , df_trunc $ time, tau_limit, 0 ), surv = c ( 0 , df_trunc $ surv, 0 , 0 ), group = df_trunc $ group[ 1 ] ) } shade_trt <- make_shade (df_trt, tau_val) shade_ctrl <- make_shade (df_ctrl, tau_val) ggplot () + # Shaded RMST areas geom_polygon ( data = shade_trt, aes (time, surv), fill = "steelblue" , alpha = 0.25 ) + geom_polygon ( data = shade_ctrl, aes (time, surv), fill = "tomato" , alpha = 0.25 ) + # KM step curves geom_step ( data = df_trt, aes (time, surv, color = "Treatment" ), linewidth = 1 ) + geom_step ( data = df_ctrl, aes (time, surv, color = "Control" ), linewidth = 1 ) + # Tau line geom_vline ( xintercept = tau_val, linetype = "dashed" , color = "black" ) + annotate ( "text" , x = tau_val - 1 , y = 0.05 , label = paste0 ( "τ = " , tau_val, " months" ), hjust = 1 , size = 3.5 ) + scale_color_manual ( name = "Group" , values = c ( "Treatment" = "cyan3" , "Control" = "tomato" ) ) + scale_x_continuous ( limits = c ( 0 , 36 ), breaks = seq ( 0 , 36 , 6 )) + scale_y_continuous ( limits = c ( 0 , 1 ), breaks = seq ( 0 , 1 , 0.2 )) + labs ( title = "RMST Visualization: KM Curves with Shaded Areas" , subtitle = paste0 ( "Shaded area = RMST up to τ = " , tau_val, " months" ), x = "Time (months)" , y = "Survival probability S(t)" ) + theme_classic ( base_size = 12 ) + theme ( legend.position = "bottom" ) KM curves with shaded RMST areas up to τ = 36 months 7.6 Interpretation Key Results Treatment group : RMST = 19 months up to \(	au\) = 36 months. Control group : RMST = 17 months up to \(	au\) = 36 months. RMST Difference : 1.9 months (95% CI: -0.22 to 4.001; p = 0.0789). Plain language : On average, patients in the treatment group survive 1.9 months longer within the first 36 months compared to the control group. This is a clinically meaningful and model-free summary of the treatment benefit — no proportional hazards assumption required. 8 References Uno H, et al. (2014). Moving beyond the hazard ratio in quantifying the between-group difference in survival analysis. Journal of Clinical Oncology . Royston P, Parmar MKB (2013). Restricted mean survival time: an alternative to the hazard ratio for the design and analysis of randomized trials with a time-to-event outcome. BMC Medical Research Methodology . Trinquart L, et al. (2016). Comparison of treatment effects measured by the hazard ratio and by the ratio of restricted mean survival times in oncology randomized controlled trials. Journal of Clinical Oncology .

title: Multi-Crossover Designs in RCTs
text: Multi-Crossover Designs in RCTs Code What you gain by adding periods — and what it costs Author Akif Mustafa ✉ Published September 11, 2026 Abstract A practical guide to multi-crossover (higher-order) randomized controlled trial designs: how they are structured, how they are analysed, what they buy you, and when they break. Table of contents Table of contents 1 Why add periods? 1.1 The standard crossover, briefly 2 Design configurations 2.1 Replicated (two-treatment) designs 2.2 Multi-treatment (Williams) designs 3 Planning a multi-crossover trial 4 Statistical considerations 4.1 Choose the estimand first 4.2 Where the variability lives 4.3 Biases to design against 4.4 Analysis methods 4.5 Handling carryover 5 What you gain 5.1 Precision, and therefore sample size 5.2 Confounding, and repeated self-control 5.3 Where the design fits 6 What it costs 6.1 Dropout and duration 6.2 Assumptions that must actually hold 6.3 Carryover survives washout more often than you’d like 6.4 Missing data gets complicated 6.5 Functional unblinding 7 Case studies 8 Summary 9 References 9.1 Trials and examples 9.2 Methodological In one paragraph. A standard crossover gives each participant two treatments in two periods. A multi-crossover design gives them three or more. That extra structure lets you estimate within-subject variability per treatment, estimate carryover instead of assuming it away, compare more than two treatments, and survive dropout. The price is a longer trial, heavier logistics, and a stricter set of assumptions. 1 Why add periods? In a parallel-group trial, each participant gets one treatment. Comparisons are made between people, so between-subject variability sits squarely in the denominator of your test statistic and inflates the sample size you need. A crossover design removes that. Each participant receives more than one treatment in a randomised order, so the comparison is made within a person. When treatment effects are fast, reversible, and repeatedly measurable, this can be dramatically more efficient. The familiar AB/BA crossover, however, is a fragile instrument. Carryover is aliased with the treatment-by-period interaction, so the two cannot be separated. A participant who drops out after the first period contributes nothing to the paired comparison. And only two treatments can be compared. Adding periods fixes much of this. That is the subject of this article. 1.1 The standard crossover, briefly Figure 1: Standard two-period, two-sequence (AB/BA) crossover. Four terms recur throughout: Period — an interval during which a participant receives and is assessed on one treatment. Sequence — the order of treatments assigned to a participant (AB, BA, ABAB, …). Washout — the gap between periods, long enough for the previous treatment’s effects to dissipate. Within-subject comparison — each participant’s response on one treatment compared against their own response on another. Table 1: What breaks in a two-period crossover, and how extra periods help. Limitation Two-Period Crossover Multi-Crossover Resolution Carryover aliased with treatment × period interaction Carryover can be tested, but only with very low power, and cannot be separated from treatment × period Extra periods break the aliasing; carryover is estimable in balanced designs Only two treatments comparable One pairwise comparison Williams and Latin Square designs handle ≥ 3 treatments Dropout after Period 1 destroys the pairing Participant contributes no within-subject information Completing ≥ 2 of ≥ 3 periods still yields within-subject comparisons No treatment-specific within-subject variance Only a pooled within-subject variance is estimable Replicated designs give a separate variance per treatment 2 Design configurations A multi-crossover (or higher-order) design is a crossover trial with three or more periods. It may involve two treatments repeated (a replicated crossover) or three or more treatments each given at least once (a multi-treatment crossover). Two closely related designs are worth naming because they appear constantly in practice: Latin Square crossover — number of periods equals number of treatments, each treatment appearing once per period across the sequence set. Williams design — a balanced Latin Square in which every treatment precedes and follows every other treatment equally often, giving balance for first-order carryover. 2.1 Replicated (two-treatment) designs Table 2: Common replicated crossover configurations for two treatments (T = test, R = reference). Design Sequences Periods What it estimates Full replicate (2×2×4) TRTR, RTRT 4 Within-subject variance for both T and R Full replicate, 4-sequence TRTR, RTRT, TRRT, RTTR 4 Within-subject variance for both T and R Partial replicate (2×3×3) TRR, RTR, RRT 3 Within-subject variance for R only Two-sequence, four-period TTRR, RRTT 4 Within-subject variance for both T and R Why replicate? Only a replicated design can estimate the within-subject variance separately for each treatment . That is exactly what reference-scaled average bioequivalence requires for highly variable drug products — which is why four-period and partial-replicate designs dominate the bioequivalence literature. 2.2 Multi-treatment (Williams) designs A Williams design is constructed so that each treatment appears equally often in each period, and each treatment is immediately preceded by every other treatment equally often. Table 3: Williams design for three treatments: six sequences, three periods. Sequence Period 1 Period 2 Period 3 Sequence 1 A B C Sequence 2 B C A Sequence 3 C A B Sequence 4 C B A Sequence 5 A C B Sequence 6 B A C For an even number of treatments t , a Williams design needs t sequences; for an odd t , it needs 2 t . So four treatments fit into a balanced 4×4 square: Table 4: Williams design for four treatments: four sequences, four periods. Sequence Period 1 Period 2 Period 3 Period 4 Sequence 1 A B C D Sequence 2 B D A C Sequence 3 C A D B Sequence 4 D C B A When the number of treatments makes full balance impractical, partially balanced designs achieve balance for a subset of comparisons — a workable compromise. A note on Balaam’s design Balaam’s design (sequences AA, AB, BA, BB) has only two periods, so it is not a multi-crossover design by the definition used here. It is included in discussions like this one because the same-treatment sequences let you estimate direct treatment and carryover effects — the same problem multi-period designs solve, tackled by adding sequences instead of periods. 3 Planning a multi-crossover trial Before analysis, five planning decisions determine whether the design will work. 1. Number of periods. Each additional period increases precision but also dropout, duration, and cost. Choose the smallest p that answers your question: 3 if you need carryover estimable or a third treatment; 4 if you need treatment-specific within-subject variances. 2. Washout duration. Set it from pharmacokinetics and pharmacodynamics, not convenience. A common rule of thumb is 5–7 elimination half-lives, but calibrate to the longest-acting treatment and to pharmacodynamic recovery, which can outlast drug clearance. In a multi-crossover design the washout must be adequate at every transition. 3. Run-in and period-specific baselines. A run-in stabilises the condition and reduces regression to the mean when participants are enrolled on extreme values. Collecting a baseline before each period gives you a direct check that participants returned to their starting state — the single most useful empirical evidence that the washout worked. 4. Sample size. For a continuous outcome, two treatments, p periods with p /2 replicates each, total participants for power \(1-\beta\) at two-sided \(\alpha\) : \[N \;=\; \frac{4\,(z_{1-\alpha/2} + z_{1-\beta})^{2}\,\sigma_w^{2}}{p\,\delta^{2}}\] which reduces to the familiar \(2(z_{1-\alpha/2}+z_{1-\beta})^2\sigma_w^2/\delta^2\) when p = 2. Inflate for anticipated dropout, and note that only \(\sigma_w^2\) appears — the between-subject variance has vanished. 5. Randomisation and simulation. Allocate with stratified permuted blocks whose block size is a multiple of the number of sequences, so period and sequence stay balanced. Because closed-form power formulae ignore dropout, carryover and unbalanced sequences, simulate the design under realistic scenarios before committing. 4 Statistical considerations 4.1 Choose the estimand first The repeated-measures structure supports several distinct quantities. Pre-specify which one you want, because it determines the model. Population-average effect — the mean difference averaged across the population. Targeted by marginal models (GEE). Relevant for treatment policy. Subject-specific effect — the difference for a given individual, or the distribution of individual effects. Targeted by mixed models. Relevant for individualised decisions. Beyond the mean effect you may care about heterogeneity of response (the treatment-by-subject interaction, which is what makes N-of-1 designs interesting) and consistency across periods (the treatment-by-period interaction, which detects tolerance, learning effects, or carryover contamination). 4.2 Where the variability lives Figure 2: Between- and within-subject variability across four periods. Crossover analysis removes the between-subject component from the treatment comparison; the extra periods let you estimate the within-subject component directly. Between-subject variance ( \(\sigma_b^2\) ) — differences in baseline level across participants. Dominates parallel-group trials; removed by within-subject differencing. Handled as a random subject effect. Within-subject variance ( \(\sigma_w^2\) ) — variation in one participant’s response to the same treatment on different occasions. This is what drives your sample size. In replicated designs it can be estimated per treatment. Period-to-period variation — temporal trends, seasonality, practice effects. Handled as a fixed period effect; biases the comparison only if the design is unbalanced. 4.3 Biases to design against Table 5: Systematic effects in multi-crossover trials, and how to handle them. It tolerates unbalanced data from dropout and yields both subject-specific and population-average estimates. Table 6: Analytical options and when each applies. Method Outcome Type Estimand Notes Linear mixed model (LMM) Continuous Subject-specific and population-average Default choice; handles missing data under MAR; assumes normal residuals Generalized linear mixed model (GLMM) Binary, count Subject-specific (conditional) Logit or log link; convergence can be fragile with small N Generalized estimating equations (GEE) Any (via link) Population-average (marginal) Needs adequate N for the sandwich estimator; no subject-specific estimates Bayesian hierarchical model Any Subject-specific, full posterior Best for small N, sparse data, and N-of-1 aggregation; prior sensitivity applies Repeated measures ANOVA Continuous Population-average within blocks Requires complete, balanced data and compound symmetry; largely superseded 4.5 Handling carryover Prevent it by design. An adequate washout, calibrated to pharmacokinetics and pharmacodynamics, is the primary safeguard. If the washout is pharmacologically defensible, the no-carryover assumption is defensible too. Assess it by analysis. In a design with sufficient degrees of freedom — a four-period replicate or a Williams design — include first-order carryover as a fixed effect in a pre-specified sensitivity analysis. If the treatment estimate barely moves, you have empirical reassurance. If it moves a lot, re-examine the washout and qualify your conclusions. Do not use the old two-stage procedure. Grizzle’s (1965) approach — test for carryover, then analyse as a crossover if non-significant and as a first-period parallel trial if significant — was dismantled by Senn (1993, 2002) on four grounds: The preliminary test has very low power, so a non-significant result is not evidence of absence. Conditioning the analysis on the test inflates the overall Type I error rate. It fails precisely when it is needed: undetected carryover leaves you with a biased crossover analysis. Reverting to first-period data discards the within-subject information that motivated the design. Critical reminder Never fall back on a first-period-only analysis because carryover was “detected”. Use a design in which carryover can be estimated directly, and report the sensitivity analysis alongside the primary one. 5 What you gain 5.1 Precision, and therefore sample size Each additional period adds within-subject replication. For a two-treatment replicated design with p periods, the variance of the treatment effect is proportional to \(1/p\) , so relative to a two-period crossover it falls as \(2/p\) . Figure 3: Variance of the treatment effect estimate relative to a two-period crossover, for two-treatment replicated designs with an even number of periods (2/p). Odd-period designs are not on this curve. Against a parallel-group trial the gain is larger still, and it scales with the intraclass correlation. Using total participants and a common effect size \(\delta\) on the total-SD scale, the ratio of crossover to parallel sample size is \((1-\text{ICC})\cdot 2/p\) . Figure 4: Total sample size for a crossover design as a proportion of the parallel-group requirement, as a function of the ICC. Ratio = (1 − ICC) × 2/p, matching the sample size formula in Section 3. For ICC between 0.5 and 0.8 — common for pharmacokinetic endpoints, physiological measurements and symptom scores — a two-period crossover needs roughly 20–50% of the parallel-group sample size, and a four-period replicate roughly 10–25% . Figure 5: Total participants for 80% power to detect δ = 0.5 total-SD units (two-sided α = 0.05), assuming ICC = 0.7, no carryover, no dropout, equal variances and perfect balance. Derived from the same formula as the curves above. This is decisive in rare diseases, paediatric subgroups and narrow phenotypes , where a parallel trial simply cannot be powered. At the limit, N-of-1 designs use repeated crossover cycles within a single patient, and aggregating several N-of-1 trials recovers population-level estimates. 5.2 Confounding, and repeated self-control Because every participant receives every treatment, there is no baseline imbalance to worry about: confounding by any stable participant-level characteristic — measured or not — is eliminated by construction. This does not extend to time-varying confounders, carryover, or differential dropout, all of which remain live threats. Repetition adds two things beyond the group mean: individual-level treatment effects , and the reproducibility of those effects across occasions, which distinguishes consistent responders from noisy ones. Multi-crossover designs lose more participants in absolute terms, but a partial completer still contributes within-subject information. Worse, if dropout is differential — participants leaving preferentially during a poorly tolerated treatment — the missing-at-random assumption behind your primary analysis fails. Clinical Setting Assumption Violated Reason Oncology (curative chemotherapy) Reversibility; disease modification Disease state is irreversibly altered Vaccine trials Reversibility (immune memory) Immune response persists; no washout is possible Surgical interventions Reversibility (structural change) Anatomical changes are permanent Gene therapy Reversibility (permanent modification) Irreversible by design Acute infections Stable disease (self-limiting) Condition resolves spontaneously Rapidly progressive neurodegeneration Stable disease (progressive) Progression between periods confounds the comparison 6.3 Carryover survives washout more often than you’d like Figure 9: First- and higher-order carryover in a four-period design. Balanced designs protect against first-order carryover, not higher-order. Three mechanisms defeat a nominally adequate washout: Pharmacodynamic persistence — enzyme induction or receptor downregulation outlasts drug clearance. Psychological carryover — the experience of one treatment colours how symptoms are perceived and reported on the next. No washout removes this. Higher-order carryover — residual effects from two or more periods back. Balanced designs distribute first-order carryover evenly; they offer no equivalent protection here. 6.4 Missing data gets complicated Figure 10: Missing data patterns in a four-period design: monotone dropout versus intermittent non-response. Pre-specify a primary analysis under MAR using mixed models, plus sensitivity analyses under MNAR — pattern-mixture models, tipping-point analyses, or controlled imputation — and a rule for handling partial period data and intercurrent events under the ICH E9(R1) estimand framework. 6.5 Functional unblinding Crossover participants can compare their own experiences across periods, which a parallel-group participant cannot. Distinct side-effect profiles, formulation differences, or a large efficacy gap can all reveal treatment identity, and the risk rises with each additional period. Mitigations — active placebo, matched formulations, double-dummy administration, objective co-primary endpoints, and a post-study blinding index (James or Bang) — reduce the problem without eliminating it. A montelukast trial in perennial allergic rhinitis ( Allergy Asthma Proc , 2008) used this structure to assess nasal congestion and sleep disturbance against placebo, with the same-treatment sequences supporting formal carryover estimation. 8 Summary Multi-crossover designs extend the standard crossover into something considerably more informative: treatment-specific within-subject variances, carryover that can be estimated rather than assumed away, more than two treatments at once, and real tolerance of dropout. That comes at a price — longer trials, harder logistics, more demanding assumptions, and a persistent risk of carryover and functional unblinding.
